description: We are Alexander Bonev, Mihail Stefanov, and Shohruh Sharifov — the team behind Geophonia. We share an interest in space, technology, and making scientific information more accessible. For the NASA Space Apps Challenge, we combined Earth visualizations, sound, and speech to help people explore our planet beyond sight.
summary:
Geophonia is an interactive web application that turns NASA Earth visualizations into an experience people can explore through sound, speech, and sight. Developed for “The Earth Information Jukebox” challenge, it makes temperature, air quality, aerosols, night lights, and lightning maps accessible beyond their visual presentation.

Users move a listening point across the map. Data values control the pitch and beating speed of a harmonic, warp-like sound, while data density controls loudness. Distinct sound profiles identify different variables, and spatial audio helps communicate location. On-demand speech reads the country or waterbody, value and unit, and selected date.

Designed with blind and low-vision users in mind, Geophonia includes keyboard navigation and a spoken, interactive tutorial. It also supports multisensory learning, helping more people discover patterns in Earth information.
details:
Geophonia translates NASA Earth visualizations into an interactive soundscape. Users explore a geographic map with a mouse, keyboard, or navigation controls, hearing how the selected information changes across locations and dates. Supported topics include temperature, air quality, aerosol types, night lights, and lightning. Users can also import regular latitude–longitude CSV grids containing their own values, units, and dates.

The application samples colors, intensity, or category information from prepared visualization images. For imported numeric grids, it samples the supplied values directly. A consistent mapping range across each dataset’s time sequence supports meaningful comparisons between frames. Image-derived estimates are clearly distinguished from numeric data, and unavailable samples are not interpreted as measured zeros.

Sonification combines several complementary signals. Values control a continuous logarithmic pitch, normally between 200 and 2,000 Hz. Nearby oscillator frequencies create acoustic beating that becomes faster as values increase. This produces a softer, warp-like sound with an additional cue for distinguishing values. Data density controls loudness, while different harmonic profiles distinguish variables and aerosol types. Spatial audio positions the listening point, and brief sounds identify shoreline crossings and map boundaries.

Phonon text-to-speech provides spoken context. Pressing 1 reads the country, ocean, or sea; 2 reads the value and unit; and 3 reads the selected date. Automatic interface announcements can be toggled independently. A guided tutorial combines visible instructions, spoken explanations, highlighted controls, and practice steps that wait for successful user actions.

Geophonia uses HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Vite, the Web Audio API, Phonon speech synthesis, NASA visualization assets, and Natural Earth geographic information. It runs in a browser and is hosted through GitHub Pages. Headphones support the spatial listening experience.

Our design priorities were keyboard access, understandable sound mappings, listening comfort, scientific transparency, and user control. The intended impact is to broaden access to Earth information for blind and low-vision users while providing an engaging, multisensory tool for education and exploration.
